verdict.rationale: Matthew 25:46 sets "eternal punishment" (kolasin aionion) in a balanced clause with "eternal life" (zoen aionion), the same adjective "eternal/age-pertaining" (aionios, G0166) governing both terminal states and the future verb "they will go away" (apeleusontai, G0565) sending one group away. The exclusion pattern recurs across the whole Bible (pan-canonical): John 3:36 ("the wrath of God abides" (orge tou theou menei), present tense (ongoing, simple statement of fact) abiding wrath), 2 Thessalonians 1:9 ("eternal destruction away from the face of the Lord" (olethron aionion apo prosopou tou kyriou)), Revelation 20:15 and 21:8 ("the lake of fire" (limne tou puros), "the second death" (thanatos deuteros, G1208)), Isaiah 66:24 and Daniel 12:2 ("reproach" (cherpah) and "abhorrence" (dera'on), H2781 H1860, lasting reproach paired with "life everlasting" (chayye olam)). The counter-pull is real and rooted in word meaning (lexical), not stylistic. The adjective "eternal/age-pertaining" (aionios) is polysemous (carries multiple senses) (Philemon 1:15 age-bounded, Jude 1:7 of Sodom's no-longer-burning fire, but 2 Corinthians 4:17-18 contrasted with "temporary" (proskairos) for lasting/durative force), and "all" or "the all" (pas / ta panta) in 1 Corinthians 15:22, Philippians 2:10-11, Romans 5:18, 1 Timothy 2:4, Colossians 1:20 admits all-without-exception, all-without-distinction, or cosmic-subjugation (bringing the whole created order under rule) readings the vocabulary itself does not rank. Verdict stands at affirms-medium because the exclusion-class pattern is denser, more lexically specific, and spread across the whole Bible (pan-canonical), while the universal-reconciliation reading exists but rests on contested word-senses.

scripture.force: Two destinies in a balanced clause: "eternal punishment" (kolasin aionion) for one group, "eternal life" (zoen aionion) for the other. The same adjective "eternal/age-pertaining" (aionios) governs both nouns in the same syntactic frame, so whatever lasting/durative or qualitative force attaches to the life of the righteous attaches in equal grammatical measure to the punishment of the others. The future verb "they will go away" (apeleusontai) is exclusion language (going away). "Punishment" (kolasis) is rare (only 2 New Testament occurrences, here and 1 John 4:18 where it pairs with "fear" (phobos), in the sense of torment or chastening), which is the lexical (word-meaning) opening universalists use to read it as remedial (corrective); the canonical balance with "life" (zoe) and the parallel adjective is the closing weight on the other side.

The wide road leads "to destruction" (eis ten apoleian, G0684), and "many" (polloi) travel it. "Destruction" (apoleia) recurs across the whole Bible (pan-canonical) as a terminal-state noun (Philippians 3:19 "whose end is destruction" (hon to telos apoleia), 2 Peter 3:7 "day of judgment and destruction of the ungodly" (hemera kriseos kai apoleias ton asebon), Revelation 17:11 "goes into destruction" (eis apoleian hupagei)), naming a class that arrives there rather than being gathered up into life.

The narrow road leads "to life" (eis ten zoen) and "few" (oligoi) are the ones who find it. The quantifiers "many" (polloi) for the wide road and "few" (oligoi) for the narrow road place the two groups in numerical opposition, which on its face is inconsistent with a final outcome in which all without exception arrive at life.

Of the present participle "the one persistently disobeying" (ho apeithon, G0544) it is said "he will not see life" (ouk opsetai zoen), and "the wrath of God abides" (orge tou theou menei, G3306, present tense, ongoing simple statement of fact) upon him. The verb "abides" (menei) describes a continuing state rather than a wrath that lapses into eventual reconciliation. The text does not say the wrath ends when faith comes; it says wrath stays on the one who keeps refusing.

The penalty is "eternal destruction" (olethron aionion, G3639, with an "from" (apo) of separation from the presence of the Lord), paid as "they will pay the just penalty" (diken tisousin). "Destruction" (olethron) occurs only 4 times in the New Testament (1 Corinthians 5:5, 1 Thessalonians 5:3, 1 Timothy 6:9, here) and in each case names a destructive judgment, never a remedial (corrective) pause. The "from the face of the Lord" (apo prosopou tou kyriou) construction makes the state an exclusion from the Lord's presence, the opposite of restored fellowship.

Anyone not found written in the book of life is cast "into the lake of fire" (eis ten limnen tou puros). "Lake" (limne) occurs only 11 times in the New Testament, of which 5 are this lake-of-fire image in Revelation; the term is technical for the final-state location. The narrative sequence places this after the great-white-throne judgment and before the new creation, making it a final, not interim, exclusion.

A named list of persons (the cowardly, faithless, abominable, murderers, sexually immoral, sorcerers, idolaters, all liars) has its "portion" (meros) in the lake burning with fire and brimstone, "the second death" (ho thanatos ho deuteros, G2288 G1208). The verse sits after the new creation announcement, so this is a final-state assignment of an excluded class outside the city.

Old Testament taproot of the two-destinies pattern. Some awake to "life everlasting" (chayye olam) and others to "reproach" (cherpah, H2781) and "lasting abhorrence" (dera'on olam, H1860). "Abhorrence" (dera'on) occurs only twice in the Hebrew canon (here and Isaiah 66:24, where the worm does not die and the fire is not quenched). The same adjective "lasting/everlasting" (olam) modifies both destinies, the Hebrew analogue to "eternal/age-pertaining" (aionios) on both sides of Matthew 25:46.

"Worm" (tola) does not die and "fire" (esh) is not quenched of the corpses of the rebels. This is the Old Testament image Mark 9:48 picks up verbatim ("the worm does not die and the fire is not quenched" (skolex ou teleuta kai to pur ou sbennutai)) and applies to Gehenna. The not-die, not-quenched pair is the canon's strongest non-cessation (does-not-end) language for the state of the excluded.

"The smoke of their torment ascends forever and ever, and they have no rest day and night" (Ho kapnos tou basanismou auton eis aionas aionon anabainei, kai ouk echousin anapausin hemeras kai nuktos). The smoke of their "torment" (basanismos) ascends "into ages of ages" (eis aionas aionon), and they have no "rest" (anapausis) day and night. This is the densest non-cessation (does-not-end) construction in the New Testament ("into ages of ages" (eis aionas aionon) plus continuous day-and-night absence of "rest" (anapausis)), repeated in Revelation 20:10 of the devil, beast, and false prophet. It tells against an annihilationist (final cessation of being) reading of the same passages and weighs heavily against a remedial (corrective) reading.

complicating_texts.resolution: "As in Adam all die, so also in Christ all will be made alive" (Hosper en to Adam pantes apothneskousin, houtos kai en to Christo pantes zoopoiethesontai). Two occurrences of "all" (pantes, G3956) are set in parallel. The universalist reading takes the second "all" (pantes) as numerically universal. The narrowing weight is "in Christ" (en to Christo) modifying the second clause, and the immediate sequel (verse 23, "each in his own order, those who are Christ's at his coming" (hekastos en to idio tagmati, hoi tou Christou en te parousia autou)) restricts the made-alive class to those who are Christ's. "To make alive" (zoopoieo, G2227) elsewhere consistently denotes the giving of resurrection life to believers (Romans 8:11, John 5:21, 1 Peter 3:18), not a universal final reconciliation. The reading remains lexically (in terms of word meaning) possible but contextually narrowed.

"Through him to reconcile all things to himself" (Di' autou apokatallaxai ta panta eis auton). "To reconcile" (apokatallasso, G0604) occurs only twice in the New Testament (here and Ephesians 2:16), so its sense cannot be triangulated from frequency. Decisively, in its only other occurrence (Ephesians 2:16) the object is "both in one body" (amphoteroi en heni somati, both Jew and Gentile in one body), a reconciliation of two groups not of every individual. The object here is the neuter "the all things" (ta panta, the things, cosmic scope including "the things in the heavens and the things on the earth" (ta en tois ouranois kai ta epi tes ges)), and the means is "having made peace through the blood of the cross" (eirenopoiesas dia tou haimatos tou staurou). The semantic field (range of meanings) admits pacification or subjugation of the whole created order rather than the conversion of every person. The verse does not require individual universal salvation, but the breadth of "the all things" (ta panta) and the near-hapax verb (a verb that occurs only once or twice in the entire Bible) keep it a real complicating datum.

"That at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord" (Hina en to onomati Iesou pan gony kampse epouranion kai epigeion kai katachthonion, kai pasa glossa exomologesetai hoti kyrios Iesous Christos). "Every knee" (pan gony, G3956 G1119) will bow and "every tongue" (pasa glossa) will confess. The universalist reads this as the universal confession of saving faith. The narrowing weight is that the lexical (word-meaning) field of "to confess/acknowledge" (exomologeo, G1843) admits both willing praise and forced acknowledgment (Isaiah 45:23 in the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint), the source text, is in an oath-court frame), and the bowing-of-knee gesture ("to bow" (kampto)) can denote vassal submission, not necessarily saving (salvific) confession. The vocabulary does not foreclose either reading, so the verse is a real complicating datum with the scope underdetermined.

"Who desires all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth" (Hos pantas anthropous thelei sothenai kai eis epignosin aletheias elthein). God wills "all people" (pantas anthropous, G3956 G0444) to be saved. The lexical (word-meaning) complication is that "wills/desires" (thelei, G2309) can carry desiderative force (what God wills as desire) or decretal force (what God brings to pass), and "all people" (pantas anthropous) can be all-without-distinction (every kind of person, fitting the immediate context verses 1-2 of praying for kings and all in authority) or all-without-exception. Neither sense is lexically (by word meaning) forced, and 1 Timothy 4:10 ("savior of all people, especially of believers" (soter panton anthropon, malista piston)) explicitly differentiates a wider and a narrower scope of "savior" (soter). The verse is genuine counter-evidence but the scope is underdetermined.

"As through one trespass condemnation came to all people, so also through one act of righteousness justification of life came to all people" (Hos di' henos paraptomatos eis pantas anthropous eis katakrima, houtos kai di' henos dikaiomatos eis pantas anthropous eis dikaiosin zoes). Through one trespass condemnation comes "to all people" (eis pantas anthropous), and through one act of righteousness "justification of life" (dikaiosin zoes) comes "to all people" (eis pantas anthropous). The parallelism of all-to-all (pantes-to-pantes) is the universalist's strongest grammatical foothold. The narrowing weight is that verse 17 ("those who receive the abundance of grace and of the gift of righteousness" (hoi ten perisseian tes charitos kai tes doreas tes dikaiosynes lambanontes)) restricts the recipients of the gift to those receiving it, and the wider canonical pattern (justification by faith, Romans 3-4) constrains the application. The verse remains a real complicating datum because the parallel is grammatical.

"Savior of all people, especially of believers" (Soter panton anthropon, malista piston). The "especially" (malista) marker creates two concentric scopes with the same noun, which can be read as God being saviour-as-rescuer of all in temporal providence and saviour-as-redeemer of believers in particular, or as universalist (with "especially" (malista) as emphatic restatement). The lexicon (the dictionary of word meanings) allows both. This is the lexical (word-meaning) model for handling "all" (pas) in salvation (soteriological) contexts.

"Sodom and Gomorrah are set forth as an example of eternal fire, undergoing the just penalty" (Sodoma kai Gomorra pros deigma puros aioniou diken hupechousai). "Eternal/age-pertaining" (aionios, G0166) modifies the fire that destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah, cities that are no longer burning. This is the universalist's strongest piece of evidence that "eternal/age-pertaining" (aionios) does not necessarily mean unending in temporal extension but can name a fire belonging to the age-to-come or fire of decisive judgment. The opposing lexical (word-meaning) weight is 2 Corinthians 4:17-18, where "eternal/age-pertaining" (aionios) is explicitly contrasted with "temporary" (proskairos, G4340), giving "eternal/age-pertaining" (aionios) a lasting/durative force in at least that frame. The adjective is genuinely polysemous (carries multiple senses) and the disambiguation is contextual, not lexical (not settled by word meaning alone). This is the lexical (word-meaning) root of the universalism debate.

"Perhaps this is why he was parted from you for a while, that you might have him back forever" (Tacha gar dia touto echoristhe pros horan hina aionion auton apeches). "Eternal/age-pertaining" (aionios) there describes a household relationship that cannot be temporally unending. The text supplies the universalist with a clearly age-bounded use of "eternal/age-pertaining" (aionios) within the same canon as Matthew 25:46. The opposing weight is that "eternal/age-pertaining" (aionios) in end-times (eschatological) contexts is repeatedly linked to incorruption, the age-to-come, and resurrection life (1 John 5:11, John 17:3, 2 Corinthians 4:18), giving it a sense the temporal use cannot displace. The polysemy (multiple senses) is real.

variants.note: No anchor verses fall in the 3 John ECM-published window (ECM apparatus = the critical edition of New Testament textual variants). Matthew 7:13-14 has minor word-order and article variants (marked in the SBLGNT apparatus) but none touch the "destruction" (apoleia) or "life" (zoe) terminus. Revelation 21:8 has lower-criticism variants in the vice list but none that remove the lake-of-fire assignment or change the "second" (deuteros) qualifier. The verdict does not turn on any contested reading.

competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: Reads "eternal/age-pertaining" (aionios) in Matthew 25:46 and 2 Thessalonians 1:9 as lasting-and-unending (anchored by the "temporary" (proskairos) contrast in 2 Corinthians 4:18 and the no-rest day-and-night construction in Revelation 14:11), takes "the one abiding" (ho menon) in John 3:36 as a persisting state of wrath on the unbeliever, and reads "torment forever and ever" (basanismos eis aionas aionon) (Revelation 14:11, 20:10) as ongoing conscious suffering. The class of the excluded remains permanently outside saving fellowship.

Reads "destruction" (apoleia, G0684), "destruction" (olethron, G3639), and "the second death" (G1208 G2288) as final cessation (end) of being rather than endless torment, drawing weight from the destruction-language frequency and from Isaiah 66:24 (corpses, not living tormented persons). Affirms the proposition under test (some are finally excluded from saving fellowship) and differs from the eternal-conscious-punishment lens only on the mode of exclusion, not on whether universalism is denied.

Reads "eternal/age-pertaining" (aionios) as age-pertaining or age-to-come quality rather than unending duration (anchored by Philemon 1:15 and the no-longer-burning fire of Jude 1:7 of Sodom). Treats "punishment" (kolasis, G2851, only 2 occurrences, paired with "fear" (phobos) in 1 John 4:18 in a chastening sense) as corrective rather than punitive. Takes the "all" (pantes) of 1 Corinthians 15:22, Philippians 2:10-11, Romans 5:18, 1 Timothy 2:4 and the "the all things" (ta panta) of Colossians 1:20 as numerically universal, weighted by the grammatical parallelism all-to-all (pantes-pantes) in Romans 5:18 and the "reconciling" (apokatallasso) of all things in Colossians 1:20 (a near-hapax verb (a verb that occurs only once or twice in the entire Bible) whose sense cannot be triangulated from frequency). Concludes that the same texts the exclusion-class lens reads as final assignment are read here as the age-of-judgment phase prior to "the restoration of all things" (apokatastasis ton panton) (Acts 3:21). The reading is a minority but lexically (in terms of word meaning) grounded option, not a category error.

hermeneutics.notes: Eternal-conscious-punishment and annihilationist lenses agree on the proposition under test (some are finally excluded) and diverge on the mode of exclusion, so the proposition is over-determined within the exclusion family. Only universal reconciliation denies the proposition, and it does so by reweighting the polysemous (multi-sense) adjective "eternal/age-pertaining" (aionios) toward Philemon 1:15 and Jude 1:7, reweighting "punishment" (kolasis) toward 1 John 4:18, and reading "all" (pas) and "the all things" (ta panta) in the salvation-scope texts as numerically universal. The lexical (word-meaning) pattern in the anchor texts is denser and more specific (the exclusion-class lens cites grammatically tight constructions like the balanced "eternal/age-pertaining" (aionios) in Matthew 25:46, the "from" (apo)-separation in 2 Thessalonians 1:9, the "portion" (meros) catalog in Revelation 21:8, and the day-and-night no-rest in Revelation 14:11), while the universalist construal rests on real but contextually ambiguous occurrences of frequent and near-hapax terms.

stem_audit.neutralized_form: Whether the final state involves a class of persons permanently excluded from saving fellowship with God, or eventual reconciliation of all persons.
stem_audit.notes: The stem is denial-framed (universalism is denied) and presumes a settled final state with two outcomes, which is itself one of the contested points. The neutralized form poses the scope of final salvation as an open question. The verdict was derived on the original stem from the lexical (word-meaning) pattern of the anchor verses (the exclusion-class shape is dense and spread across the whole Bible (pan-canonical)), with the "restoration" (apokatastasis) and "all" / "the all things" (pas / ta panta) texts weighed as real complicating data. Confidence remains medium rather than high because "eternal/age-pertaining" (aionios) is polysemous (carries multiple senses) (Philemon 1:15 and Jude 1:7 against 2 Corinthians 4:18), "punishment" (kolasis) is a near-hapax (a word that occurs only once or twice in the entire Bible) (only 2 occurrences, 1 John 4:18 in a chastening sense), "to reconcile" (apokatallasso) is also a near-hapax (Colossians 1:20 and Ephesians 2:16), and "all" (pas) in the salvation-scope verses admits the all-without-exception versus all-without-distinction versus cosmic-subjugation (whole created order brought under rule) senses that the words alone do not rank.

lay_summary: The question asks whether the New Testament words point to some persons being finally shut out from fellowship with God, rather than every person eventually saved. The strongest single piece of word-evidence is Matthew 25:46, where one Greek adjective, "eternal/age-pertaining" (aionios), governs both halves of the sentence in a balanced clause. The righteous go into eternal life and the others go into eternal punishment, and because the same word covers both, whatever lasting quality the life has, the punishment has in equal grammatical measure. The verb means they go away, the language of being sent off, not of being brought back. The same shape recurs across the canon. In John 3:36 the one who keeps refusing the Son will not see life, and the wrath of God stays on him in the present tense (ongoing, simple statement of fact). In 2 Thessalonians 1:9 the penalty is eternal destruction, defined as being away from the presence of the Lord. In Revelation 20:15 and 21:8 a class is assigned to the lake of fire, called the second death, after the new creation is announced. The Old Testament root is in Daniel 12:2 and Isaiah 66:24, where some awake to lasting life and others to lasting reproach, and the worm of the corpses does not die and the fire is not quenched. There is a real counter-current that must be weighed honestly. The adjective "eternal/age-pertaining" (aionios) carries multiple senses (it is polysemous) in the canon itself. In Philemon 1:15 it describes a household relationship that cannot be temporally unending, and in Jude 1:7 it describes the fire of Sodom, cities that are no longer burning. That gives the minority reading a foothold to take aionios as age-pertaining or age-to-come quality rather than unending duration. "Punishment" (kolasis), the word in Matthew 25:46, occurs only twice in the New Testament, and the other occurrence (1 John 4:18) pairs it with "fear" (phobos) in a chastening sense, which gives an opening to read it as corrective. The reconciliation verbs are scarce: "to reconcile" (apokatallasso) occurs only twice, and in its other occurrence (Ephesians 2:16) the object is two groups (Jew and Gentile) made one body, not every individual. The word "all" (pas) in 1 Corinthians 15:22, Philippians 2:10-11, Romans 5:18, 1 Timothy 2:4, and Colossians 1:20 admits at least three readings the vocabulary does not rank: every individual, every kind of person, or the whole cosmic order put in its place. The exclusion-class pattern is denser, more specific, and spread across the whole Bible. The universalist construal exists, rests on real multiple senses of frequent and near-hapax words, and is a minority but lexically (word-meaning) grounded option. The verdict supports the proposition that not all are finally saved, at medium confidence because the words alone do not close the scope question.
